opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, the biggest change is that it closes the gap between having an idea and being able to test it.

In racing, especially on the engineering side, you're always working against the clock. Between sessions you might have an hour, sometimes less, to go through data, talk to the driver, and decide what to change on the car. Before, if I had a hunch about something, say how tyre temperatures were evolving over a stint or whether a particular corner was costing us time, I often didn't have time to write the analysis properly. I'd either rely on gut feel or park it for after the weekend.

With tools like ChatGPT and Codex, I can sketch out what I want, get a working script quickly, and then spend my time on what actually matters: checking whether the result makes sense and deciding what to do with it. I'm not handing over the engineering judgment. I'm handing over a lot of the plumbing that used to sit between me and the answer.

It's also changed who gets to contribute. Racing has always been quite hierarchical in terms of who has the specialist skills. Now someone who understands the car really well but isn't a software person can build their own tools, explore the data themselves, and bring something concrete to the conversation. That's powerful for younger engineers, and for anyone coming into the sport from a less traditional route.

There's a responsibility that comes with that, though. In motorsport, a wrong number can mean a wrong decision on the pit wall, so you have to stay sceptical. You verify the output, you sanity-check it against what the driver is telling you and what the physics says, and you never let the tool be the final word. Used that way, I think it lets us ask more questions, try more ideas, and ultimately go faster.

r001.rationale: The response says AI closes the gap between having an idea and testing it, and lets Joyce sketch out an idea and get a working script or tool quickly.

r002.rationale: It says more people can contribute despite racing’s hierarchy, but does not say AI helps Joyce avoid persuading others who might dismiss her ideas as far-fetched.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the biggest shift is how much of the grind they take off my plate. In racing, so much of the value is in the data: tire degradation curves, fuel strategy, lap-by-lap telemetry, weather windows. Historically, if I wanted to ask a real question of that data, I either needed an engineer with spare time, which never exists on a race weekend, or I had to teach myself enough scripting to hack something together at midnight in the hotel.

Now with Codex, I can describe what I want in plain language. Something like, "Pull every stint where the ambient temperature dropped more than three degrees and show me how the rear tire delta changed." A few minutes later I've got a working script and a chart I can actually bring into the debrief. It doesn't replace the engineers, but it means I show up to the conversation with a hypothesis instead of a hunch.

ChatGPT fills a different gap for me. It's the thinking partner in the gaps between sessions. I'll talk through a setup change, or a regulation I don't fully understand, or how to explain a technical issue to a sponsor without losing them. It helps me sharpen the argument before I take it to the team.

The thing I'd caution about, and I say this to younger drivers and junior engineers constantly, is that the tool is only as good as the question. If you don't understand what a tire is doing physically, the model will happily give you a confident answer that's wrong for your car. So I treat it as an accelerator for people who already know the sport, not a shortcut around learning it.

Where I think it really changes what I can contribute is breadth. I came in as a driver. I'm not a trained data scientist. But now I can genuinely participate in strategy, in simulation work, even in some of the aero conversations, because the barrier to interrogating the data has mostly fallen away. That makes me a more useful member of the team than my job title suggests, and I think that's going to be true for a lot of people in motorsport over the next few years.

r001.rationale: She says she can describe a racing data question in plain language and get a working script and chart, whereas previously she needed an engineer or scripting skills.

r002.rationale: The response describes bringing hypotheses into team conversations, but does not say AI frees her from persuading people who might dismiss her ideas as far-fetched.

astra-6.text:
I think they can help me turn an idea into something useful much more quickly. In racing, you’re constantly asking questions about what happened, why it happened, and what you could do differently. Tools like ChatGPT and Codex could help me explore those questions, work through data, or build a small tool without having to do every step from scratch.

That gives me more room to contribute my judgment—to decide which questions matter and whether the answers make sense. I’d still want to check anything we relied on, but it opens up what I can try and how quickly I can learn.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the tools can help her turn an idea into something useful much more quickly and build a small tool, clearly describing a means to realize racing ideas.

r002.rationale: The candidate says AI frees her to contribute her judgment and explore questions, but does not mention persuading others or their dismissing her ideas as far-fetched.

I can see ChatGPT helping me work through questions and explain what I’m seeing, while Codex could help me build tools to explore those ideas. That would let me contribute beyond the skills I already have, while still bringing my own judgment and experience to the decisions.
